solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Around start of week, comes to call

indicators.note: the amount word is placed around the start of the week, enclosing it

parts.note: a bill that comes to a figure sums to it; SUMS
Monday, the day that opens the working week, abbreviated MON

explanation.surface: Someone arrives near the beginning of the week to pay a visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes to' reads as arriving, but it is a verb meaning 'totals'.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: to call someone to court or to a meeting is to issue a formal order to attend.

clue.text: Reserved a little turkey, ultimately for stuffing sort of kebab

indicators.note: the kebab word is used for stuffing, taking the letter inside it

parts.note: a shish kebab is meat grilled on a skewer

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of the bird

explanation.surface: A cook who held back a bit of turkey to fill a kebab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserved' looks like 'kept back', but it means shy.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym with a softening suffix: slightly bashful or timid, reserved only to a small degree.

clue.text: Old PM's official staff shortened press article

definitions.note: read as 'Old PM is', the 's linking to the wordplay

indicators.note: the ceremonial rod is shortened, losing its last letter

parts.note: a mace is a staff carried as a symbol of office
a mill is a machine that presses or grinds
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A former prime minister's team cut a newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' is a rod, not employees; 'shortened' trims MACE to MAC. Harold Macmillan was UK prime minister 1957-63.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Harold Macmillan was a Conservative British prime minister from 1957 to 1963.

clue.text: Foul that almost incapacitated rugby player

indicators.note: something incapacitated is put out of order, so these letters are disordered
almost the whole word, lacking its final letter

explanation.surface: A foul on the rugby pitch that nearly put a player out of action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims THAT to THA, and 'incapacitated' jumbles FOUL with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: in rugby union this back, also called fly-half or stand-off, links scrum-half and three-quarters.

clue.text: Singer at first mischievously being interested only in number one

definitions.text: being interested only in number one

indicators.note: only the first letter of the performer word is wanted

parts.note: elfishly means in an impish, mischievous way

explanation.surface: A vocalist playing pranks while caring only about getting a chart-topping hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number one' looks like a chart hit; here it is oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: looking after number one means putting yourself first, which is acting with self-regard.

clue.text: What's removed by girl approaching Bond?

parts.note: something approaching is getting nigh, near
a tie is a bond or link

explanation.surface: A spy-film scene: what a girl takes off as James Bond draws near.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' wants to be 007, but it is a plain synonym for a tie.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a night garment is what a woman takes off, especially in the suggestive picture of a Bond girl.

clue.text: Nick? He died a rich man

parts.note: to nick is to steal or arrest, nab
OB, for Latin obiit, means he died, as on gravestones

explanation.surface: Someone asks about Nick, a wealthy man who has passed away.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a man of great wealth, originally a governor in Mughal India who returned home rich.

clue.text: Amount of money used on publicity is relative

parts.note: a grand is a thousand pounds or dollars
an ad, advertisement, is publicity

explanation.surface: The marketing budget is proportional, a comment on advertising spend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relative' reads as an adjective (comparative) but is a noun, a family member.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a grandfather is a family member, one kind of relative.

clue.text: Northern region where dynamic economy picked up

indicators.note: picked up as by a listener's ear, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a fast-growing economy is called a tiger economy

explanation.surface: An area in the north where a booming economy has recovered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' looks like 'recovered'; it signals a sound-alike. A tiger economy is a fast-growing one.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this is the belt of coniferous forest across subarctic Russia and Canada, a northern zone.

clue.text: In which mercury's rising — I see it's fantastic outside?

definitions.text: In which mercury's rising — I see it's fantastic outside?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go outside, around, the chemical symbol
fantastic means wild and fanciful, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of I SEE IT, the 's read as 'is' linking to fantastic

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read upwards, backwards

parts.note: Hg is the chemical symbol for mercury

explanation.surface: Someone checks the thermometer, sees the mercury climbing and remarks on the fantastic weather outside.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a temperature in the eighties (Fahrenheit) is when the mercury climbs. 'rising' signals the upward reading in this down entry; 'fantastic' and 'outside' do the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a reading from eighty to eighty-nine degrees Fahrenheit is hot weather, when a thermometer's column has climbed high.

clue.text: Group of sailors in bay, turning, awkwardly clutch packs

indicators.note: the turned word packs, holds inside it, the rearranged letters
the bay is turned round, its letters read backwards
the word clutch is handled awkwardly, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Sailors in a bay clumsily grabbing at things as their boat swings round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is only a link; 'turning', 'awkwardly' and 'packs' are the three signals, the turned bay word wrapping round the jumbled grip.
explanation.definitionFit: A yachting society is an organised body of people who sail, so a group of sailors.

clue.text: A test for internet connection is taking off

parts.note: a ping is a network signal sent to see if a machine responds

explanation.surface: Someone describing a quick check that their broadband is working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking off' is mimicking, not leaving the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: taking someone off means impersonating them, copying their manner as a mimic does.

clue.text: Bright star showing some perspicacity

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the long word are used, a run within it

explanation.surface: A clever person is called a bright star for their shrewdness.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this is the brightest star in the constellation Virgo, one of the most brilliant in the sky.

clue.text: Unfavourably cast?

parts.note: to take something this way is to take it unfavourably; an actor unfavourably cast is put in a poor role

explanation.surface: An actor complaining about a poor role.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means 'unfavourably' (take a remark this way), and read literally it is an actor given a bad role.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: taking a remark this way means taking offence; literally, an actor given a poor role is badly cast.

clue.text: Like continental estate, perhaps, bequeathed to present doctor I have

parts.note: something bequeathed in a will is left to someone
to present something is to hand it over
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: A European country house left in a will to a GP, who claims it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'estate' is a car (an estate car, a station wagon), not land; cars made for mainland Europe have the steering wheel on the left.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a car built for mainland European roads has its steering on the left, so an estate car from there is like this.

clue.text: Philosopher's last letter: hence it's treated specially

definitions.note: read as 'Philosopher is', the 's linking to the wordplay

indicators.note: the letters are treated in a special way, given a new arrangement

parts.note: Z is the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A thinker's final letter, which is therefore handled with special care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last letter' looks like a final piece of correspondence; it is Z, mixed in with HENCE ITS.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Friedrich Nietzsche was a 19th-century German thinker, author of Thus Spoke Zarathustra.

clue.text: What waiter brings from distance to pour?

parts.note: ice is coldness of manner, aloofness or distance
to bucket, or bucket down, is to pour with rain

explanation.surface: A puzzle over what a waiter fetches from far off to serve the drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distance' and 'to pour' look like serving instructions; they are separate synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a waiter brings a container of chilled water to keep wine or champagne cold at the table.

clue.text: Contemptuous of banality in science fiction, endlessly dull

indicators.note: the banality word goes in the science fiction abbreviation

parts.note: corn is trite, banal sentimentality

indicators.note: with both ends removed, leaving the middle

explanation.surface: A critic sneering at clichés in science fiction that drags on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' reads as 'forever', but it strips the ends from DULL to give UL.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: showing disdain or scorn for something, holding it in low regard.

clue.text: Cryptic clue maybe not about verse in pop song

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go about, surround, the abbreviation for verse
cryptic means puzzling and obscure, so the words that follow are scrambled

explanation.surface: A puzzle-maker's admission that a clue is perhaps not about poetry within a pop song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic' jumbles CLUE MAYBE NOT to CANTBUYMELOE, and 'about' puts V inside it. The answer is a 1964 Beatles song.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this 1964 Beatles number is a chart single, so a pop song.

clue.text: More like a man to mess up?

definitions.meaning: the comparative of butch, more manly in appearance
to botch or bungle a job, hack it about

explanation.walkthrough: One meaning is 'more butch', the comparative adjective; the other is the verb for making a hash of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the comparative of a word for manly, and a verb meaning to ruin a job by clumsiness.

clue.text: Cockney judge at hearing does perhaps for female pensioner?

indicators.note: London Cockney speech drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: to hold is to judge or consider, as in 'I hold that'

indicators.note: at a hearing the word is heard, so it is a sound-alike

parts.note: does, female deer, are an example of deer

explanation.surface: A Cockney judge at a court hearing does something for an elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'does' reads as a verb but is the plural of doe. 'hearing' looks like a court hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquialism: an elderly woman is affectionately or patronisingly called this, so a female pensioner fits.

clue.text: Coward's fan of the Sun, on reflection blessed!

indicators.note: a reflection shows the image the other way round, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: Noel Coward's song says mad dogs and Englishmen go out in the midday sun

explanation.surface: An exclamation praising a sun-lover in a Noel Coward song after some thought.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward's song 'Mad Dogs and Englishmen' says they go out in the midday sun; 'blessed!' is a mild oath.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphemism: 'blessed!' is used as a mild curse in exclamations, much like a soft form of 'damned'.

clue.text: Advanced as far as old man with unknown mineral

parts.note: something that advanced rose up
to, as in 'from here to there'
pa is a familiar word for father, one's old man
Z is a letter used for an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: A prospector's father who made progress with an unidentified gem.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this pinkish variety of the gemstone is a natural crystalline mineral.

clue.text: Short exercise to occupy room?

definitions.meaning: a knee bend done in the gym, crouching and rising
to live in an empty building without permission

explanation.surface: A brief workout done to fill a space.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: stocky, a crouching exercise, and taking over property illegally.
explanation.definitionFit: Three senses: stocky in build, a crouch-and-rise exercise, and occupying an empty building unlawfully.

clue.text: Regularly presented product by trying to look sexy?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter

explanation.surface: An advertising model presenting a product while vamping for the camera.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: pushing the lips out in a sultry pout is what models do when trying to seem alluring.

clue.text: Harsh introduction to Olympics for European runner

parts.note: dour means stern, severe, harsh

indicators.note: the introduction to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A tough start to the Games for a sprinter from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runner' is a river, which runs; this one flows through Spain and Portugal to Porto.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword convention: a river runs, and this one flows across Iberia, so it is a European runner.

clue.text: Look ashamed, maybe even promising hand with money

definitions.meaning: to go red in the face, blush
in poker, a hand of cards all of one suit, which a player holds hopefully
having plenty of cash, well off

explanation.surface: A card player blushing over a good hand and a stack of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: to redden, the poker hand of one suit, and well supplied with cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Three senses of one word: reddening with shame, a poker hand of a single suit, and having plenty of cash.

clue.text: Countries joined together to vet journalist for free

parts.note: the UN, United Nations, is a union of countries
to vet is to check
ED, editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: An international body uniting to screen a reporter for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for free' reads as 'at no cost', but 'free' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: something left unrestrained runs free, without control or restriction.

clue.text: Before short drive with Yankee, books service

indicators.note: the books come before the rest in the answer

parts.note: lit, literature, is books collectively

indicators.note: the word for drive is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: to drive someone on is to urge them
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A trip in the car with an American friend, preceded by some reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims URGE to URG.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: the set form of public worship in a church is a service.

clue.text: Slip back, saying nothing about arrival

indicators.note: the whole assembled word is read back to front
the silent word goes about, around, the arrival abbreviation

parts.note: someone saying nothing is mute
ARR is the abbreviation for arrival, as on timetables

explanation.surface: Someone slipping in at the back, keeping quiet about when they turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slip back' looks like one phrase; 'Slip' is the definition and 'back' reverses the whole container built by 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a printed error, a slip in a text, often listed in a correction slip.
